Hi Lauren / Ben —

Thanks for running through the pilot constraints this morning. Quick recap from our side and a few clarifying questions so we can align internal engineering capacity: 

- Goal: sustain 120 concurrent streaming sessions during peak (US-East) with p95 tail latency <= 350ms for first byte and steady-state token latency <= 80ms.
- Typical session pattern: 8–12 messages per session, avg 220 tokens generated per message, ~30% of sessions use streaming responses.
- Traffic profile: 09:00–11:30 and 16:00–18:30 local — bursts up to 2.8x baseline for ~10–15 minutes.

Questions for Redwood:
1) Can you confirm how connection pooling and multiplexing affect the per-session concurrency accounting? Do 120 parallel sessions map to 120 connections or can we reuse fewer sockets with multiplexing?
2) For burst windows, what burst credits or short‑term overage policy applies? We may need a temporary uplift for the pilot's first two weeks.
3) Any recommendations for prompt-side batching/early-answer strategies to hit the p95 SLA while keeping token cost reasonable?

Attached a snapshot of our current traffic sample and a draft SLO doc we used internally. We'll be ready to move to a timeboxed pilot once we have a rate/credit proposal.

Hi Alice — thanks for the clear summary and the sample traffic — very helpful. Short answers below, then proposed next steps.

1) Connection multiplexing: Redwood supports socket multiplexing for WebSocket and HTTP/2 clients. Multiplexing lets you serve multiple logical sessions over fewer TCP connections without increasing per-session token cost. For accounting, we track active sessions (logical streams) rather than raw sockets — so your 120 concurrent sessions map to ~120 active logical streams; you can run them over as few as 20–40 physical connections depending on client-side limits and keep-alive behavior.

2) Burst credits: For pilots we offer a scoped burst window (up to 3x baseline for 30 minutes) with an auto-throttled fallback. We can offer a two-week pilot uplift: +50% concurrency buffer and a one-time 100k token credit to absorb initial spikes. After the pilot, steady-state pricing/quotas apply.

3) Prompt batching & latency: For short-turn dialogues we suggest token streaming + prefix caching for repeated system prompts and early token flush (send partial tokens to client). Also consider a small local response cache for predictable prompts (e.g., status-check endpoints). Aditya has an optimization checklist attached below.

Next steps:
- Ben will follow up with a formal ratecard and pilot quote (today).
- Aditya will validate the multiplexing assumptions against your client SDK and share a recommended connection sizing table.
- If that looks good, we'll spin up a timeboxed Dedicated pilot for two weeks.

I'll attach a tailored SLO proposal and Redwood ratecard to this thread.

— Lauren

Hi all — quick technical note after I reviewed your traffic sample. Two concrete suggestions that should keep you under the p95 target without over-allocating capacity: 

1) Connection sizing table (recommended):
   - If you use HTTP/2 multiplexing: 8–12 logical sessions per connection comfortably, so ~15–20 sockets will cover 120 sessions with headroom.
   - If you must rely on individual WebSocket connections (no multiplexing): plan for ~120 sockets; consider an intermediate proxy to aggregate connections.

2) Streaming knobs to hit p95:
   - Enable prefix/KV caching for repeated system prompts (saves ~40–60ms on first‑token).
   - Use 8–16 token generation chunks for initial streaming flush; this keeps first‑byte latency low while allowing the model to warm KV cache.

I also ran a quick simulation against the burst profile you sent — with prefix caching and 50% pilot uplift we stay under 350ms p95 for first token in ~88% of simulated windows; tail events still require the burst credit we discussed.

I'll attach the connection-sizing CSV and a short script to measure effective logical stream counts from your client logs. Happy to jump on a quick call if you want me to walk through it.

— Aditya
